screens.question: You scrape your knee. Before your body knows whether a germ entered, what might tell it something is wrong?

options.text: The exact name of a germ

screens.reveal: Nearby injured cells can be the clue. Let’s see why your body can notice them so quickly.

image.prompt: A small scrape on a knee, shown in a simple cutaway. Show several nearby cells just beneath the broken skin. Keep the scrape and cells easy to distinguish; no text labels.
image.alt: A small scrape breaks the skin above nearby cells.

screens.title: Cells on watch
screens.text: Some cells in your skin help defend you. They are **immune cells**. Like watchguards, they look for signs of trouble rather than a germ’s name.
screens.exampleLineIdea: a scrape that puts watchguard cells near injured skin cells

image.prompt: Simple skin cutaway with one watchguard-like immune cell beside several ordinary skin cells. Label the cells “immune cell” and “skin cells.” Show the immune cell watching its surroundings, with no uniform or human face.
image.alt: An immune cell sits beside ordinary skin cells and watches for signs of trouble.

screens.title: Spot the shared mark
screens.text: Two different bacteria can carry the same kind of mark on their outer surfaces. Bacteria are one kind of **microbe**, or tiny germ. A watchguard can spot that shared mark like a familiar uniform, without reading a name tag.
screens.exampleLineIdea: recognizing the same team uniform on different players

image.prompt: Two clearly different-looking bacteria, each with the same small outer-surface feature highlighted in yellow. Label the highlighted feature on each “shared mark.” Show no names for the bacteria.
image.alt: Two different bacteria have the same highlighted mark on their outer surfaces.

screens.context: A watchguard cell encounters several different bacteria.
screens.question: Which clue could it notice early?

options.text: A feature shared by the bacteria
options.reason: You can spot the same outer feature on different bacteria without knowing exactly which bacterium each one is.

options.text: The exact name of one bacterium
options.reason: A name would identify one bacterium, but this early watchguard looks for shared signs instead.

options.text: Whether the bacteria have already caused a fever
options.reason: A fever might happen later. The watchguard can notice a shared outer feature before then.

screens.title: Damage is a clue
screens.text: A cell hurt by a splinter can give off a sign of damage, even if no germ entered. A watchguard can notice it like a smoke alarm sensing smoke: it detects trouble without knowing the exact cause.
screens.exampleLineIdea: a splinter that hurts skin even when no germ enters

image.prompt: Simple diagram: an injured skin cell on the left and a microbe on the right. Each sends a different visible sign toward the same watchguard immune cell in the center. Label the signs “damage sign” and “microbe sign.”
image.alt: An injured cell and a microbe send different signs toward the same watchguard cell.

screens.title: Send a warning
screens.text: When a watchguard notices a sign, it can warn nearby cells. This quick, broad response is part of **innate defense**—your body’s first watch, not a germ ID check. The warning flags possible trouble; it does not prove a germ is there.
screens.exampleLineIdea: nearby skin cells receiving a warning after a scrape

image.prompt: Simple skin cutaway showing one watchguard immune cell sending a visible signal toward several neighboring cells. Label the signal “warning.” Do not show a named germ or imply the signal identifies one.
image.alt: A watchguard immune cell sends a warning signal to nearby cells.

screens.context: A watchguard cell is near a new cut.
screens.question: Which situations could lead it to warn nearby cells?

options.text: Damaged cells or a microbe with a recognizable outer feature
options.reason: You have two possible clues: signs from injured cells and features shared by microbes. Either can lead to an early warning.

options.text: Only a germ whose exact identity is known
options.reason: An exact identity is tempting because it sounds certain, but the watchguard can act on broader signs.

options.text: Only damaged cells, never a microbe’s outer feature
options.reason: Damaged cells can be a clue, but you can also recognize a shared feature on a microbe.

screens.context: While pulling weeds in your backyard, you get a small splinter. It breaks your skin and hurts nearby cells.
screens.question: What might a watchguard notice, and why could it warn nearby cells before knowing whether a germ entered?

options.text: Signs from the hurt cells; they flag possible trouble without proving a germ entered.
options.reason: You can have injured cells even without a germ. Their signs give the watchguard a reason to warn nearby cells.

options.text: The splinter’s exact name; that proves a germ entered.
options.reason: A splinter’s name tells you nothing about whether a germ entered. The hurt cells provide the early clue.

options.text: Nothing yet; it must identify a germ before it can warn anyone.
options.reason: It is tempting to wait for certainty, but the watchguard can warn nearby cells when it notices signs of damage.

image.prompt: A close-up cutaway of a hand after pulling weeds: a small splinter breaks the skin, with nearby injured cells and one watchguard immune cell beneath the surface. Label “splinter,” “injured cells,” and “watchguard cell.” Do not show a germ.
image.alt: A splinter breaks the skin near injured cells and a watchguard immune cell.

summary: Some immune cells act like watchguards, looking for signs of trouble rather than a germ’s exact identity.
A watchguard can notice an outer feature shared by different microbes.
Injured cells can also give off signs of damage, even when no germ is present.
A watchguard can warn nearby cells about possible trouble without proving that a germ entered.
